notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What is the difference between undefined, unspecified and implementation-defined behaviour in C?
notes.back:
• Undefined Behaviour (UB): the standard imposes no requirements. The compiler may assume it never happens and optimise on that assumption (signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, data races, strict-aliasing violations).
  • Unspecified: several outcomes are allowed and the implementation need not document which (evaluation order of function arguments).
  • Implementation-defined: the implementation chooses and must document it (sizeof(int), signedness of char, right shift of a negative value).
In kernel and firmware code there is no safety net: UB becomes silent memory corruption or a security hole.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What does the compiler assume about int overflow, and how does the Linux kernel deal with that?
notes.back:
Signed overflow is Undefined Behaviour (UB), so the optimiser assumes it never happens: if (x + 1 < x) folds to false, int loop counters are assumed not to wrap.
Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2^N.
The kernel builds with -fno-strict-overflow (GCC: equivalent to -fwrapv -fwrapv-pointer), which defines signed wrap as two's complement.
Portable code: test before the operation, or use __builtin_add_overflow() (kernel wrapper: check_add_overflow()).

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front:
uint16_t x = 0xFFFF;
uint32_t y = x * x;
What is wrong on a target with 32-bit int? What happens on a 16-bit int microcontroller?
notes.back:
Integer promotion: any operand of rank below int (char, short, uint8_t, uint16_t, bitfields) is converted to int if int can hold all its values, otherwise to unsigned int.
  • 32-bit int: both operands become signed int; 0xFFFF * 0xFFFF = 0xFFFE0001 > INT_MAX → signed overflow → Undefined Behaviour.
  • 16-bit int (AVR, MSP430): uint16_t is unsigned int; the product wraps to 0x0001 before widening. Defined, but wrong.
Fix for both: (uint32_t)x * x.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: if (-1 < 1U): which branch is taken, and what real-world bug class does this cause?
notes.back:
False. Usual arithmetic conversions: with equal rank, the signed operand converts to unsigned, so -1 becomes UINT_MAX.
Bug class: signed lengths.
int len = user_len;
if (len > MAX)          /* negative len passes */
        return -EINVAL;
memcpy(dst, src, len);  /* converted to size_t: huge copy */
Any comparison against sizeof silently becomes unsigned. Use size_t/u32 for lengths and build with -Wsign-compare.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: State the strict aliasing rule. Which accesses are exempt, and what does the kernel do about it?
notes.back:
An object may only be accessed through an lvalue of: its effective type, a qualified version of it, its signed/unsigned counterpart, an aggregate or union containing such a member, or a character type.
Anything else is Undefined Behaviour: the compiler may assume an int * and a float * never alias and cache or reorder loads and stores.
The exemption is one-way: any object may be read through unsigned char *, but a char buf[] may not be read through a uint32_t *.
The kernel builds with -fno-strict-aliasing; much firmware does as well. Otherwise use memcpy().

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: Give two correct ways to reinterpret the bits of a float as a uint32_t. Which common way is wrong?
notes.back:
uint32_t u;
memcpy(&u, &f, sizeof u);       /* always valid; compiles to one move */

union { float f; uint32_t u; } p = { .f = f };
u = p.u;                        /* valid in C (not in C++) */
Wrong: *(uint32_t *)&f. That is a strict-aliasing violation, and in the general case also a potential alignment fault.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What exactly does volatile guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?
notes.back:
Guarantees: every read and write in the source becomes an actual load/store, in source order, never cached in a register, never elided.
Does not give:
  • atomicity (v++ is still load, add, store)
  • mutual exclusion
  • memory barriers or ordering between CPUs
  • cache coherency for Direct Memory Access (DMA) buffers
Legitimate uses: Memory-Mapped Input/Output (MMIO) registers, variables shared with an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) or signal handler, locals that must survive longjmp().

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: Why does the kernel documentation call volatile "considered harmful"? What is used instead?
notes.back:
Shared kernel data is protected by locks, atomics or Read-Copy-Update (RCU), which already force correct accesses. volatile on the declaration pessimises every access and hides the real concurrency design.
Instead:
  • Memory-Mapped Input/Output (MMIO): readl()/writel() on __iomem pointers
  • a single lockless access: READ_ONCE() / WRITE_ONCE() (volatile at the access, not the declaration)
  • busy-wait: cpu_relax()
  • counters: atomic_t, refcount_t
Accepted exceptions: jiffies, and some memory that a device modifies behind the CPU's back.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What does restrict promise, and who pays if the promise is broken?
notes.back:
restrict on a pointer promises that, for the lifetime of that pointer, the object it points to is accessed only through it (or pointers derived from it). The compiler may then skip reloads and vectorise.
Breaking the promise is Undefined Behaviour; nothing is diagnosed.
memcpy(void *restrict d, const void *restrict s, size_t n): overlapping buffers are UB, which is why memmove() exists.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: Read: const char *p, char *const p, const char *const p. What happens if you cast away const and write?
notes.back:
Read right to left: pointer to const char (cannot write through p); const pointer to char (cannot reseat p); both.
Writing through a cast-away const is Undefined Behaviour only if the object itself was defined const. In practice:
  • kernel: object lives in write-protected .rodata → page fault / oops
  • microcontroller: object lives in flash → write ignored or bus fault
const on a pointer parameter is a promise by the callee, not a guarantee that the data does not change: another alias may still modify it.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front:
Which of these are Undefined Behaviour?
i = i++ + 1;
a[i] = i++;
f(i++, i++);
i = i + 1;
notes.back:
The first three: an object is modified twice, or modified and separately read, with no sequence point in between (unsequenced side effects). The last is fine.
Related but only unspecified: whether g() or h() runs first in f(g(), h()).
Sequence points: end of a full expression, &&, ||, ?:, the comma operator, and after argument evaluation just before a call.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: List the undefined and implementation-defined cases of the C shift operators. Why is the kernel's BIT(n) defined as (1UL << (n))?
notes.back:
Undefined Behaviour:
  • count negative or ≥ width of the promoted left operand
  • left shift of a negative value
  • left shift of a signed value whose result is not representable (1 << 31 with 32-bit int)
Implementation-defined: right shift of a negative value (arithmetic shift on every relevant Application Binary Interface (ABI)).
1U << 31 is fine, hence the unsigned constant. For bits ≥ 32 use BIT_ULL(n) / 1ULL << n: 1UL << 40 is UB on a 32-bit target.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front:
uint8_t b[4];
uint64_t v = b[0] | b[1] << 8 | b[2] << 16 | b[3] << 24;
Find the bug.
notes.back:
b[3] is promoted to signed int. If b[3] >= 0x80, b[3] << 24 shifts into the sign bit (Undefined Behaviour; in practice a negative int). Converting that to uint64_t sign-extends, so the upper 32 bits become all ones.
Fix: (uint32_t)b[3] << 24.
Kernel: get_unaligned_le32(b).

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What are the rules for valid pointer arithmetic and pointer comparison?
notes.back:
• Arithmetic is valid only inside one array object (a single object counts as an array of 1) or to one-past-the-end; one-past may not be dereferenced. Merely forming a pointer outside that range is Undefined Behaviour.
  • < and > only between pointers into the same object; == between any.
  • Subtraction: same array; result type ptrdiff_t.
  • Arithmetic on void * is a GNU extension (element size 1), used all over the kernel.
  • Pointer ↔ integer conversion is implementation-defined; use uintptr_t (kernel: unsigned long).

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front:
struct sock *sk = tun->sk;
if (!tun)
        return POLLERR;
Why was this an exploitable kernel bug (CVE-2009-1897), and what build flag resulted?
notes.back:
tun is dereferenced before the check, so the compiler infers tun != NULL (otherwise Undefined Behaviour) and deletes the check. With page zero mapped by user space, the kernel carried on using an attacker-controlled structure.
Fixes: check before dereferencing; the kernel builds with -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks; mmap_min_addr prevents mapping page 0.
Lesson: UB is not "whatever the hardware does". The optimiser reasons backwards from it.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: When does an array not decay to a pointer? What is sizeof(buf) inside void f(char buf[64])?
notes.back:
No decay when the array is the operand of sizeof, _Alignof, typeof, unary & (yields char (*)[64]), or when a string literal initialises an array.
In a parameter list char buf[64] is adjusted to char *buf, so sizeof(buf) is the pointer size (4 or 8).
That is why the kernel's ARRAY_SIZE() includes __must_be_array(), which breaks the build when given a pointer.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What are the meanings of static in C, and what does -fno-common change?
notes.back:
• File scope: internal linkage. The default for every driver-internal function and variable: no namespace pollution, and the compiler can inline or drop it.
  • Block scope: static storage duration. One instance in .data/.bss that keeps its value. Makes the function non-reentrant.
  • void f(int a[static 4]): caller guarantees at least 4 elements (rare).
-fno-common (default since GCC 10): a tentative definition int x; appearing in two files is a multiple-definition link error instead of being silently merged. Put extern int x; in the header and one definition in a .c file.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: A driver fills a stack struct member by member and then copy_to_user()s it. What is the vulnerability?
notes.back:
Padding bytes and any unassigned members still hold stale kernel stack contents → information leak (defeats Kernel Address Space Layout Randomisation (KASLR), may leak keys).
= {0} and designated initialisers zero the members; padding is not guaranteed to be zeroed.
Fix: memset(&s, 0, sizeof(s)) before filling, or lay out the struct with no implicit padding (explicit __u32 reserved;).
Hardening: CONFIG_INIT_STACK_ALL_ZERO (-ftrivial-auto-var-init=zero). Objects with static storage duration are always zero-initialised.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What is a flexible array member? How is it allocated safely in the kernel, and why were [0] and [1] trailing arrays purged?
notes.back:
struct msg {
        u32 len;
        u8  data[];     /* C99; must be the last member */
};
m = kmalloc(struct_size(m, data, n), GFP_KERNEL);
sizeof(struct msg) excludes data. struct_size() saturates to SIZE_MAX on overflow, so the allocation fails instead of being too small.
[0] (GNU) and [1] (C89 hack) defeat compiler bounds checking (-fstrict-flex-arrays=3, FORTIFY_SOURCE, __counted_by(len)), and [1] makes sizeof off by one element.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: Why are C bitfields avoided for hardware registers and wire formats?
notes.back:
Implementation-defined: bit order within the storage unit, whether fields straddle units, the storage unit's type and alignment, signedness of a plain int bitfield.
Additionally:
  • access width is not guaranteed; the register may demand a 32-bit access while the compiler emits a byte access
  • each assignment is a separate read-modify-write: non-atomic, several bus writes where hardware wants one, and it clobbers write-1-to-clear bits
  • adjacent bitfields share a storage unit, so two contexts writing different fields still race
Use masks and shifts: GENMASK(), FIELD_PREP(), FIELD_GET().

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What is the underlying type of an enum, and why is -fshort-enums an Application Binary Interface (ABI) hazard?
notes.back:
Enumeration constants have type int; the enumerated type is an implementation-defined integer type able to hold all values.
-fshort-enums picks the smallest such type. Bare-metal ARM toolchains (arm-none-eabi) commonly default to variable-size enums, while Linux ABIs use int.
Mixing objects built with different settings changes struct layouts and argument sizes silently. The linker warning "uses variable-size enums yet the output is to use 32-bit enums" is the symptom, typically with a vendor binary library.
Never put an enum in a wire format or a user-space ABI struct; use a fixed-width integer.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: Is plain char signed? How has that bitten portable kernel and embedded code?
notes.back:
Implementation-defined. x86: signed. ARM, PowerPC, RISC-V: unsigned.
Typical bugs: if (c < 0), c == EOF, char used as an array index (negative index), sign extension in int x = c; for bytes ≥ 0x80. The code works on the x86 workstation and breaks on the ARM target, or vice versa.
Since Linux 6.2 the kernel builds with -funsigned-char on all architectures.
Use u8/uint8_t for bytes and char only for text.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What are the ILP32, LP64 and LLP64 data models? Which assumption does Linux kernel code rely on?
notes.back:
• ILP32: int, long, pointer are 32-bit (32-bit Linux, most 32-bit microcontrollers)
  • LP64: long and pointer are 64-bit, int 32 (64-bit Linux, BSD, macOS)
  • LLP64: only long long and pointer are 64-bit (Windows)
Kernel invariant: sizeof(long) == sizeof(void *), so unsigned long is the pointer-sized integer.
Use u8/u16/u32/u64 for hardware and fixed layouts, __u32 etc. in user-visible (uapi) headers, size_t for sizes. Never put long or a pointer in an ioctl struct: 32-bit user space on a 64-bit kernel sees a different layout.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: How does C express polymorphism in the kernel? Show the pattern.
notes.back:
A const struct of function pointers (an "ops table"), filled with designated initialisers, plus a pointer to it in the object:
static const struct file_operations foo_fops = {
        .owner          = THIS_MODULE,
        .open           = foo_open,
        .read           = foo_read,
        .unlocked_ioctl = foo_ioctl,
};
Unset members are NULL; the core checks before calling or substitutes a default.
const places the table in read-only memory, so it cannot be overwritten to hijack control flow. The "derived" object is recovered with container_of().

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: Why is static inline the idiom for functions in headers? What goes wrong with plain inline?
notes.back:
C99 plain inline gives an inline definition only: no external symbol is emitted. If the compiler decides not to inline (for example at -O0), the link fails with an undefined reference unless exactly one translation unit also declares it extern inline. GNU89 semantics were the reverse.
static inline avoids the issue: each translation unit gets a private copy if one is needed.
inline is only a hint. Kernel: __always_inline where correctness depends on inlining, noinline to keep a separate stack frame.
Prefer it to function-like macros: type checking and single evaluation of arguments.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: Why wrap multi-statement macros in do { ... } while (0)? What is a GNU statement expression, and which problem does it solve?
notes.back:
do { } while (0) makes the macro a single statement that requires a ;, so if (x) FOO(); else ... parses correctly.
A statement expression ({ ...; value; }) lets a macro declare temporaries and yield a value, so each argument is evaluated once:
#define min(a, b) ({            \
        typeof(a) _a = (a);     \
        typeof(b) _b = (b);     \
        _a < _b ? _a : _b; })
The naive ((a) < (b) ? (a) : (b)) evaluates an argument twice: min(i++, j), or min(readl(reg), x) reading a read-to-clear register twice.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What do # and ## do in a macro, and why is the two-level __stringify() needed?
notes.back:
#x turns the argument into a string literal; a##b pastes tokens.
Arguments that are operands of # or ## are not macro-expanded first:
#define __stringify_1(x) #x
#define __stringify(x)   __stringify_1(x)

__stringify_1(PAGE_SIZE)   /* "PAGE_SIZE" */
__stringify(PAGE_SIZE)     /* "4096"      */
Token pasting generates families of symbols from one definition (initcall entries, per-register accessor functions, X-macro tables).

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What is the lifetime of a compound literal such as (struct pt){ .x = 1 }?
notes.back:
• At file scope: static storage duration.
  • Inside a function: automatic storage, living until the end of the enclosing block. It is not a temporary that dies at the end of the expression.
So p = &(struct pt){1, 2}; is valid for the rest of the block, but returning it, or using it after the block ends, is a dangling pointer.
Handy for passing a one-off struct or array argument: f((int[]){1, 2, 3}, 3);

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: Why are Variable Length Arrays (VLAs) banned from the kernel, and what replaced them?
notes.back:
• The kernel stack is small and fixed (8 to 16 KiB); a VLA sized from user input is a stack overflow primitive.
  • alloca-like code is slower than a fixed-size array.
  • Stack-depth analysis becomes impossible.
The kernel has been VLA-free since 4.20 and builds with -Wvla. Replacements: a fixed worst-case array, or kmalloc().
On a microcontroller the argument is stronger: no Memory Management Unit (MMU) means no guard page, so an overflow silently corrupts .bss or the heap.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: How do you check an invariant at compile time in C11 and in the kernel? Give a typical driver use.
notes.back:
C11: _Static_assert(expr, "message"); (static_assert via <assert.h>).
Kernel: BUILD_BUG_ON(cond) breaks the build when cond is true; static_assert() is also available. BUILD_BUG_ON_ZERO() works inside expressions.
Typical use: pin down a hardware or Application Binary Interface (ABI) layout so a refactor cannot silently break it:
static_assert(sizeof(struct foo_desc) == 16);
static_assert(offsetof(struct foo_regs, irq_status) == 0x20);

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: memcpy() vs memmove(): what is the rule, and how does it bite in driver code?
notes.back:
memcpy() with overlapping source and destination is Undefined Behaviour (the parameters are restrict). memmove() handles overlap.
Trap: shifting data inside a single buffer (dropping a consumed header from a receive buffer, inserting into an array) overlaps by construction → memmove().
For Memory-Mapped Input/Output (MMIO) regions use neither: memcpy_toio() / memcpy_fromio(). The optimised memcpy() may use access widths, unaligned accesses or instructions that device memory does not tolerate.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front:
for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)
        process(a[i]);
What happens?
notes.back:
i >= 0 is always true for an unsigned type. After i == 0, i-- wraps to SIZE_MAX → out-of-bounds access and an endless loop. With n == 0 the first index is already SIZE_MAX.
Correct idiom:
for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; )
        process(a[i]);
-Wtype-limits (part of -Wextra) reports the always-true comparison.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What happens when an out-of-range value is converted to a signed integer type? What did C23 change about integer representation?
notes.back:
Conversion to a signed type that cannot represent the value is implementation-defined (or raises an implementation-defined signal), not undefined. Every mainstream compiler truncates modulo 2^N.
Conversion to an unsigned type is always defined: modulo 2^N.
C23 mandates two's complement. Earlier standards also allowed ones' complement and sign-magnitude. Signed arithmetic overflow remains Undefined Behaviour in C23.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: printk("%d\n", val) where val is u64: what is wrong, and which formats does kernel code use for u64, size_t, phys_addr_t and dma_addr_t?
notes.back:
Variadic arguments undergo only the default argument promotions (small integers → int, float → double). A specifier/argument mismatch is Undefined Behaviour; on 32-bit targets a 64-bit argument also misaligns every argument after it.
  • u64: %llu / %llx
  • size_t: %zu; ssize_t: %zd
  • phys_addr_t: %pa (pass by reference: &addr)
  • dma_addr_t: %pad
__printf(1, 2) (__attribute__((format))) makes the compiler check custom logging functions.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What are offsetof, _Alignof and _Alignas, and where do drivers need them?
notes.back:
• offsetof(type, member): byte offset of a member; the basis of container_of() and of layout assertions for register blocks.
  • _Alignof(type): required alignment; a power of two.
  • _Alignas(n): raise an object's alignment. GNU spelling: __attribute__((aligned(n))); kernel: __aligned(n), ____cacheline_aligned.
Driver uses: Direct Memory Access (DMA) descriptors that hardware requires on 8/16/64-byte boundaries, buffers aligned to the cache line for cache maintenance, per-CPU data kept on separate cache lines.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Language Core and Undefined Behaviour
notes.front: What are the ways to end up with a dangling pointer in C, and which one is specific to interrupt or callback driven code?
notes.back:
• returning or storing the address of an automatic variable
  • use after free() / kfree()
  • a compound literal or block-scope object used after its block ends
  • realloc() moving the block while old pointers are still held
Specific to asynchronous code: handing a pointer to a stack object to something that outlives the function: a timer, a work item, a Direct Memory Access (DMA) transfer, a queued message. The function returns, the frame is reused, and the callback or the hardware writes into someone else's stack.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front:
struct a { char c1; int i; char c2; };
struct b { int i; char c1; char c2; };
What are the sizes on a typical 32/64-bit Application Binary Interface (ABI), and why? Which tool shows struct holes in kernel objects?
notes.back:
struct a: 12 bytes. c1 (1) + 3 padding + i (4) + c2 (1) + 3 tail padding.
struct b: 8 bytes. i (4) + c1 + c2 + 2 tail padding.
Rules: each member is placed at a multiple of its own alignment; the struct's alignment is that of its strictest member; tail padding makes sizeof a multiple of that, so arrays of the struct stay aligned.
Ordering members from largest to smallest alignment minimises padding.
Tool: pahole (reads DWARF debug info) prints offsets, holes and cache-line boundaries.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: What does __attribute__((packed)) do, and what are its hazards?
notes.back:
Removes padding and sets the struct's alignment to 1, so members may sit at unaligned addresses.
  • Access through the struct is safe: the compiler emits byte-wise or unaligned-capable code (slower).
  • Taking the address of a member and using it as a normal u32 * is not: the alignment information is lost (-Waddress-of-packed-member).
  • Unaligned access cost varies: fine on x86; always faults on Cortex-M0; configurable trap on Cortex-M3/M4; on ARMv7-A some instructions cannot do it.
Kernel helpers: get_unaligned(), put_unaligned(), get_unaligned_le32().
Use __packed only for layouts dictated by hardware or a protocol.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front:
Why is this a bad way to parse a packet, and what is the robust way?
struct hdr *h = (struct hdr *)buf;
len = h->length;
notes.back:
Four independent problems:
  • alignment: buf may not satisfy the alignment of struct hdr
  • aliasing: a char array read through a struct hdr lvalue
  • endianness: the wire order may differ from the CPU
  • padding: the compiler's layout may not match the wire layout
Robust: assemble fields from bytes (get_unaligned_be16(buf + 2)), or memcpy() into a local struct with explicitly sized, endian-annotated members and then convert.
The kernel frequently does cast, but only onto __packed structs with __be16/__le32 members, and it builds with -fno-strict-aliasing.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: How does kernel code handle endianness, and how are mistakes caught at build time?
notes.back:
Conversion helpers: cpu_to_le32(), le32_to_cpu(), cpu_to_be16(), be16_to_cpu(), etc. They compile to nothing when the CPU already matches.
Annotated types: __le16, __le32, __be32... are __bitwise types. The static checker sparse (make C=1) reports mixing them with plain integers or with each other without a conversion.
Rule: data in device-visible or on-wire structures uses __leXX/__beXX; convert exactly once at the boundary.
Network byte order is big-endian. PCI and USB are little-endian.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: x86-64 System V calling convention: which registers carry arguments, which are callee-saved, and why does the kernel build with -mno-red-zone?
notes.back:
• Integer/pointer arguments: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9, the rest on the stack. Return value: rax.
  • Callee-saved: rbx, rbp, r12 to r15. Everything else is caller-saved.
  • Stack is 16-byte aligned at the call instruction.
Red zone: a leaf function may use the 128 bytes below rsp without moving rsp. In the kernel an interrupt or exception pushes its frame onto the same stack and would overwrite that area, so the kernel disables it with -mno-red-zone.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: ARM Procedure Call Standard (AAPCS, 32-bit): argument registers, callee-saved registers, stack alignment. Why does it matter for Cortex-M interrupt handlers?
notes.back:
• Arguments and return value: r0 to r3 (64-bit values in r0:r1); further arguments on the stack.
  • Callee-saved: r4 to r11, plus sp. lr holds the return address; r12 is scratch.
  • Stack: 8-byte aligned at public interfaces.
On exception entry, Cortex-M hardware pushes exactly the caller-saved set (r0-r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR). Therefore an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) is an ordinary C function: no assembly wrapper and no special attribute.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: How large is a kernel stack, and what coding constraints follow from that?
notes.back:
Fixed per thread: 16 KiB on x86-64 and arm64, 8 KiB on 32-bit ARM. It does not grow.
Consequences:
  • no large local buffers (a char buf[1024] is already questionable): use kmalloc()
  • no unbounded recursion
  • no Variable Length Arrays (VLAs) or alloca()
  • -Wframe-larger-than= warns per function; scripts/checkstack.pl lists offenders
CONFIG_VMAP_STACK puts stacks in vmalloc space with guard pages, so an overflow faults immediately instead of corrupting a neighbour. Side effect: stack memory must not be used for Direct Memory Access (DMA).

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: Name the main sections of a C program image. In firmware, what is the difference between the Load Memory Address (LMA) and Virtual Memory Address (VMA) of .data?
notes.back:
• .text: code
  • .rodata: const objects, string literals
  • .data: initialised writable objects
  • .bss: zero-initialised objects; occupies no space in the image
  • heap and stack: carved out of the remaining RAM by the linker script
On a microcontroller .text and .rodata execute in place from flash. .data must run in RAM (VMA) but its initial values are stored in flash (LMA). Startup code copies LMA → VMA and zeroes .bss before main().
Linker script: .data : { ... } > RAM AT > FLASH.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: The kernel has no malloc(). What are the allocators and how do you choose between them?
notes.back:
• kmalloc(size, gfp): slab-backed, physically contiguous, fast; for small objects (the practical limit is a few MiB, in reality use it for kilobytes). kzalloc() zeroes. kcalloc()/kmalloc_array() check n * size for overflow.
  • vmalloc(size): virtually contiguous only; for large buffers; may sleep; not directly usable for Direct Memory Access (DMA).
  • kvmalloc(): tries kmalloc, falls back to vmalloc; free with kvfree().
  • kmem_cache_create(): dedicated slab cache for many same-sized objects.
  • dma_alloc_coherent(): for buffers shared with a device.
  • alloc_pages(): whole pages.
Every allocation can fail: always check for NULL.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: What do the allocation flags GFP_KERNEL, GFP_ATOMIC and GFP_NOWAIT mean? What happens if you get it wrong?
notes.back:
"GFP" stands for Get Free Pages.
  • GFP_KERNEL: may sleep to reclaim memory or do Input/Output. Process context only, with no spinlock held.
  • GFP_ATOMIC: never sleeps and may dip into emergency reserves. For interrupt handlers and code under a spinlock. Fails more readily.
  • GFP_NOWAIT: never sleeps, no access to the reserves.
GFP_KERNEL in atomic context produces "BUG: sleeping function called from invalid context" (with CONFIG_DEBUG_ATOMIC_SLEEP) or a deadlock.
Better design: allocate in probe() or process context, and only use the memory in the interrupt path.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: A driver deals with three kinds of address. Name them and the rules for each.
notes.back:
• Kernel virtual address (void *): what the CPU dereferences.
  • Physical address (phys_addr_t): what the memory controller sees. Never dereferenced; it must be mapped first (ioremap() for device registers, kmap/memremap() for memory).
  • Bus / Direct Memory Access (DMA) address (dma_addr_t): what the device puts on the bus. It may differ from the physical address because of an Input-Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) or bus offsets.
virt_to_phys() is valid only for the kernel's linear mapping (kmalloc memory), not for vmalloc, stack or ioremap addresses. Only addresses returned by the DMA mapping API may be given to a device.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: Why may a driver not simply dereference a pointer passed from user space? What does it use instead?
notes.back:
• The pointer may be invalid, unmapped or swapped out: the access must be able to fault and recover.
  • It may point into kernel memory: a confused-deputy read or write.
  • Hardware enforces the separation: Supervisor Mode Access Prevention (SMAP, x86) and Privileged Access Never (PAN, ARM) fault on a direct access.
Use copy_from_user() / copy_to_user(). They return the number of bytes not copied, so non-zero means return -EFAULT. For scalars: get_user() / put_user().
The __user annotation lets sparse flag direct dereferences.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: What is a double fetch (Time-Of-Check to Time-Of-Use (TOCTOU)) bug in an ioctl handler?
notes.back:
get_user(len, &uarg->len);
if (len > MAX) return -EINVAL;
...
copy_from_user(&k, uarg, sizeof(k));
memcpy(dst, k.data, k.len);      /* second fetch of len */
User space can change uarg->len from another thread between the two fetches, so the validated value is not the value used.
Rule: copy the whole argument into kernel memory once, then validate and use only the kernel copy.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: What is false sharing, and which kernel annotations address it?
notes.back:
Two CPUs write different variables that happen to share one cache line (typically 64 bytes). Each write invalidates the other CPU's copy; the line bounces between cores and throughput collapses even though there is no logical sharing.
Remedies:
  • ____cacheline_aligned / ____cacheline_aligned_in_smp on hot members or structs
  • group read-mostly fields apart from frequently written ones (__read_mostly)
  • per-CPU variables for counters
pahole shows where cache-line boundaries fall within a struct.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: Memory-Mapped Input/Output (MMIO) vs port Input/Output: what is the difference, and what does a driver use for each?
notes.back:
• MMIO: device registers appear in the physical address space. Map with ioremap() (or devm_ioremap_resource()), access with readb/w/l/q() and writeb/w/l/q(). Universal on ARM and RISC-V; used by PCI Express devices everywhere.
  • Port I/O: separate x86 address space reached with the in/out instructions: inb(), outb(), after request_region(). Legacy devices.
ioread32()/iowrite32() with pci_iomap() work for both.
Device mappings are created uncached and with device memory attributes; ordinary RAM mappings are not. That is one reason a physical register address cannot just be cast to a pointer.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: Why is floating point forbidden in kernel code, and what is the escape hatch?
notes.back:
On kernel entry only the integer registers are saved. The Floating-Point Unit (FPU) / vector state still belongs to the interrupted user task, so kernel code using it would corrupt user-space state. Saving it on every entry would be too expensive.
The kernel is built with flags such as -mno-sse / -mgeneral-regs-only, so accidental use fails to compile.
Escape hatch: kernel_fpu_begin() ... kernel_fpu_end() on x86, kernel_neon_begin() on ARM. Used for crypto and RAID code. Preemption is disabled inside and sleeping is not allowed.
Otherwise: fixed-point integer arithmetic.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: What are PAGE_SIZE, PAGE_SHIFT and PAGE_MASK? Why must driver code not hard-code 4096?
notes.back:
PAGE_SIZE == 1UL << PAGE_SHIFT; PAGE_MASK == ~(PAGE_SIZE - 1).
Helpers: PAGE_ALIGN(x) rounds up; offset_in_page(p); x >> PAGE_SHIFT gives a Page Frame Number (PFN).
The page size is a build-time architecture choice: arm64 supports 4, 16 and 64 KiB; PowerPC commonly uses 64 KiB. Drivers that assume 4096 break mmap() handlers, scatter-gather lists and ring sizing on those systems.
The general power-of-two idiom: ALIGN(x, a) = (x + a - 1) & ~(a - 1).

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Memory, Layout and the ABI
notes.front: What is an object's effective type, and why does it matter for memory obtained from an allocator or a raw buffer?
notes.back:
For a declared object, the effective type is its declared type. Allocated memory has none until it is written: the first store through a non-character lvalue sets the effective type for subsequent reads.
Consequences:
  • allocator memory may be used as any type, and re-used as another after being rewritten
  • a declared char buf[N] keeps type char; reading it through a u32 * violates strict aliasing even when the alignment is fine. memcpy() out of it is always valid.
Custom pool and arena allocators in firmware are usually built on a char array, which is one more reason such projects use -fno-strict-aliasing.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: Name the stages from .c to a running image, the file type each produces, and what a translation unit is.
notes.back:
• Preprocess (cpp, gcc -E): expands #include and macros → .i. That output is the translation unit: one .c file with all of its headers.
  • Compile (cc1, gcc -S): → assembly .s
  • Assemble (as, gcc -c): → relocatable object .o in Executable and Linkable Format (ELF)
  • Link (ld): resolves symbols, applies relocations and places sections according to the linker script → ELF executable, or for the kernel vmlinux / a .ko module
  • Firmware only: objcopy -O binary / -O ihex strips ELF down to a flashable image
The compiler sees one translation unit at a time; cross-file knowledge comes only from declarations, unless Link Time Optimisation (LTO) is enabled.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: What is the difference between a hosted and a freestanding C implementation? What may you still rely on with -ffreestanding -nostdlib?
notes.back:
Hosted: full standard library, and the program starts at main(). Freestanding (kernels, bare-metal firmware): no library, and the entry point is implementation-defined.
Headers that are still guaranteed (C11): <stddef.h>, <stdint.h>, <limits.h>, <stdarg.h>, <stdbool.h>, <float.h>, <iso646.h>, <stdalign.h>, <stdnoreturn.h>. They contain only types and macros.
Catch: GCC and Clang still emit calls to memcpy, memmove, memset and memcmp (struct assignment, large initialisers), and to libgcc helpers such as __aeabi_uldivmod for 64-bit division on 32-bit ARM. You must provide them. The kernel provides its own and uses do_div() / div_u64() for 64-bit division.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: What happens between reset and main() on an ARM Cortex-M microcontroller?
notes.back:
• Hardware loads the initial Main Stack Pointer (MSP) from vector table word 0 and the program counter from word 1 (the reset handler). The table sits at address 0 by default.
  • Reset_Handler:
  • copy .data initial values from flash to RAM
  • zero .bss
  • SystemInit(): clocks, flash wait states, Floating-Point Unit (FPU) enable, Vector Table Offset Register (VTOR)
  • __libc_init_array(): constructors
  • call main(); if it returns, loop forever
Until .data/.bss are set up, C code must not touch globals. A stack pointer is all that C fundamentally needs, which Cortex-M hardware provides, so the reset handler itself can be written in C.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: How does C code use symbols defined in a linker script, for example _sbss and _ebss?
notes.back:
A linker symbol is an address with no storage behind it. Declare it as an object and use only its address:
extern uint32_t _sbss, _ebss;

for (uint32_t *p = &_sbss; p < &_ebss; p++)
        *p = 0;
Reading _sbss as a value would fetch whatever happens to be stored at the start of .bss.
The kernel uses the same mechanism for __init_begin, __start___ex_table, the initcall arrays, and so on, usually declared as extern char name[];.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: What is a weak symbol, and how do embedded startup files and the kernel use it?
notes.back:
A weak definition (__attribute__((weak)), kernel __weak) is overridden at link time by any strong definition of the same name, without a duplicate-symbol error.
  • Startup files: every Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) name in the vector table is a weak alias of Default_Handler (an endless loop). Defining void USART1_IRQHandler(void) in your own code replaces it.
  • Kernel: architecture-overridable defaults, for example __weak functions in generic code that an architecture may reimplement.
Trap: misspell the handler name and the link still succeeds; the interrupt lands in Default_Handler and the system appears to hang.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: What do -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wl,--gc-sections do, and why does the vector table need KEEP()?
notes.back:
The compiler places every function and object in its own section (.text.foo, .data.bar); the linker then discards every section not reachable from the entry point. This gives significant flash savings with vendor libraries.
Nothing in the C code references the vector table; only the hardware reads it. Without KEEP(*(.isr_vector)) in the linker script it is garbage-collected and the chip does not boot.
The same applies to anything found only via section iteration: init tables, command tables. The kernel's linker script uses KEEP() for its initcall and __ksymtab sections for that reason.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: What does __attribute__((section("name"))) enable? Explain __init and how module_init() works for built-in code.
notes.back:
It places a function or object in a named section. Combined with linker-script start/end symbols, the linker builds an array with no central registry.
  • __init → .init.text, __initdata → .init.data: freed after boot ("Freeing unused kernel memory"). Calling an __init function later is a use-after-free, which modpost reports as a section mismatch.
  • For built-in code module_init(fn) stores fn in an .initcallN.init section; do_initcalls() iterates over them in level order (core, postcore, arch, subsys, fs, device, late). module_init maps to device level.
  • For a loadable module, module_init(fn) aliases fn to init_module.
Firmware uses the same trick for shell command tables and driver registries.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: Which C dialect and which semantics-changing compiler flags does the Linux kernel build with?
notes.back:
Dialect: -std=gnu11 since 5.18 (previously gnu89). GNU extensions are used freely: typeof, statement expressions, __attribute__, case ranges, void * arithmetic.
Flags that turn Undefined Behaviour into defined behaviour:
  • -fno-strict-aliasing
  • -fno-strict-overflow (signed and pointer wrap are defined)
  • -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks
  • -funsigned-char (since 6.2)
Others: -fno-common, -fno-PIE, -mno-red-zone (x86-64), no floating point/vector code generation, -Wvla, -fstack-protector-strong, -ftrivial-auto-var-init=zero (when configured).
-O0 is not supported: the code relies on inlining and dead-code elimination.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: What are likely() / unlikely(), and when should a driver use them?
notes.back:
#define likely(x) __builtin_expect(!!(x), 1). It tells the compiler which branch to lay out as the fall-through path, keeping the hot path contiguous and moving the cold path away.
It affects code layout, not the CPU's dynamic branch predictor.
Use only for error paths and conditions that really are heavily skewed, in hot code. A wrong annotation is worse than none. IS_ERR() already contains unlikely().

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: What is __attribute__((cleanup(fn))), and how does the kernel (6.5+) use it?
notes.back:
When the annotated variable goes out of scope, fn(&var) is called: scope-based resource management in C.
Kernel wrappers in <linux/cleanup.h>:
struct foo *f __free(kfree) = kzalloc(sizeof(*f), GFP_KERNEL);
if (!f)
        return -ENOMEM;

guard(mutex)(&dev->lock);       /* unlocked on every return path */
...
return_ptr(f);                  /* hand ownership out, skip cleanup */
It removes a class of goto-unwind mistakes (a missed unlock, a leak on an early return).
Rule: define and initialise the variable in the same statement, and do not mix this style with goto cleanup in one function.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: What are nm, objdump, readelf, size, addr2line and the linker map file used for?
notes.back:
• nm: symbol table. T/t text, D/d data, B/b bss, U undefined, W weak; upper case means global.
  • objdump -d / -S: disassembly, optionally interleaved with source. -h: section headers with Load Memory Address (LMA) and Virtual Memory Address (VMA).
  • readelf -S -l -r: sections, segments, relocations.
  • size: text/data/bss totals. Flash use ≈ text + data; static RAM use ≈ data + bss.
  • addr2line -e vmlinux <addr>: address → file:line. For kernel oops lines use scripts/faddr2line with func+0x1c/0x80.
  • Map file (-Wl,-Map=out.map): where every section of every object landed, and why it was pulled in.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: What kind of file is a .ko kernel module, and what does loading it involve? What do EXPORT_SYMBOL and EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL do?
notes.back:
A .ko is a relocatable Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) object, i.e. not fully linked. The module loader:
  • allocates memory and copies the sections
  • resolves undefined symbols against the kernel's exported symbol table
  • applies relocations
  • checks vermagic and, with CONFIG_MODVERSIONS, symbol checksums
  • runs the module's init function
Only symbols marked EXPORT_SYMBOL() are visible to modules; EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL() only to modules declaring a GPL-compatible MODULE_LICENSE. A proprietary licence string taints the kernel.
Hence the usual failure mode: "Unknown symbol in module".

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: What is sparse, and which annotations does it check?
notes.back:
A semantic checker for kernel C, run with make C=1 (or C=2 to check all files).
  • __user: user-space pointer; no direct dereference
  • __iomem: Memory-Mapped Input/Output (MMIO) cookie; accessors only
  • __percpu, __rcu: separate address spaces
  • __bitwise types (__le32, __be16, gfp_t): no mixing without conversion
  • __must_hold(l), __acquires(l), __releases(l): lock balance
In a normal compile these expand to nothing; under sparse they become address-space and context attributes. They give C a few extra type-system dimensions at no run-time cost.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: How do you cross-compile the kernel or a module? What is the difference between the arm-none-eabi- and aarch64-linux-gnu- toolchains?
notes.back:
make ARCH=arm64 CROSS_COMPILE=aarch64-linux-gnu- defconfig Image modules dtbs
make -C <kernel-build-dir> M=$PWD ARCH=arm64 CROSS_COMPILE=... modules
Triplet: arch-vendor-os-abi.
  • arm-none-eabi-: no operating system; bare-metal Embedded Application Binary Interface (EABI); ships newlib. For microcontroller firmware.
  • arm-linux-gnueabihf-, aarch64-linux-gnu-: target Linux with glibc. For user space and, by convention, the kernel (which uses no libc anyway).
An out-of-tree module must be built against the exact configured kernel tree it will be loaded into; otherwise vermagic or symbol versions mismatch.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: How do you get printf() working on a bare-metal newlib target, and what does it cost?
notes.back:
newlib implements printf() on top of stubs that you provide ("retargeting"):
int _write(int fd, const char *buf, int len)
{
        for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)
                uart_putc(buf[i]);
        return len;
}
Also _sbrk() (heap growth for malloc()), _read, _close, _fstat, _isatty, _lseek. --specs=nosys.specs supplies dummy versions; --specs=nano.specs selects the small newlib-nano.
Cost: tens of KiB of flash with float formatting, hundreds of bytes of stack, possible heap use, not reentrant by default, and it blocks on the Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter (UART). Never call it from an interrupt handler.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front:
Why does a busy-wait delay loop vanish at -O2, and what are the correct alternatives?
for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++)
        ;
notes.back:
The loop has no observable side effect, so the optimiser removes it. Making i volatile keeps it, but the duration still depends on the compiler, flags, clock and flash wait states.
Alternatives:
  • a hardware timer or SysTick-based delay_ms()
  • a calibrated cycle counter (Data Watchpoint and Trace (DWT) CYCCNT on Cortex-M3 and above)
  • kernel: udelay() / mdelay() for calibrated busy-waits; usleep_range() / msleep() when sleeping is allowed
General lesson: code that works at -O0 and fails at -O2 almost always has a missing volatile, a race, or Undefined Behaviour.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Compiler, Linker and Startup
notes.front: IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_FOO) vs #ifdef CONFIG_FOO: why does the kernel prefer the former inside functions?
notes.back:
if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_FOO))
        foo_setup(dev);
IS_ENABLED() expands to a constant 1 or 0 (it is true for both =y and =m). Both branches are parsed and type-checked in every configuration, then the dead branch is eliminated. The code cannot bit-rot in rarely built configurations.
#ifdef hides code from the compiler entirely and fragments the control flow.
Requirement: declarations used in the dead branch must still be visible, so headers provide static inline stubs when the option is off. #ifdef remains necessary around struct members and whole function definitions.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: What is a data race in C11 terms, and what is the consequence? Which kernel tool detects them?
notes.back:
Two accesses to the same object from different threads of execution, at least one of them a write, with no synchronisation and not both atomic. In C11 that is Undefined Behaviour.
Practical consequences: torn reads and writes, a value re-loaded halfway through a computation, stores invented or merged by the compiler, stale values kept in registers.
An Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) versus the main loop on a single core counts as well: it is concurrency without parallelism.
Tool: Kernel Concurrency Sanitizer (KCSAN), which sets watchpoints on sampled accesses and reports concurrent conflicting ones.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: What do READ_ONCE() and WRITE_ONCE() do, and which compiler transformations do they prevent?
notes.back:
They perform the access through a volatile-qualified lvalue, so exactly one load or store is emitted, at that point in the code.
Prevented:
  • refetching: p = ptr; if (p) use(p); compiled as two loads of ptr, with the second possibly NULL
  • load/store tearing: one access split into several smaller ones
  • invented stores: the variable used as scratch space before its final store
  • fusing of repeated loads in a polling loop
They provide no atomicity for read-modify-write and no ordering between CPUs. They also document to KCSAN and to readers that the access is deliberately lockless.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: barrier() vs mb() / rmb() / wmb() / smp_mb(): which problem does each solve? How do x86 and ARM differ?
notes.back:
• barrier(): a compiler barrier. Stops the optimiser from moving or merging accesses across that point. Emits no instruction.
  • mb(), rmb(), wmb(): CPU memory barriers. Force the ordering of loads and stores as observed by other CPUs or by devices. smp_*() variants reduce to barrier() on uniprocessor builds.
x86 has Total Store Order (TSO): only a store followed by a load may be reordered, so smp_rmb()/smp_wmb() are just barrier(), while smp_mb() is a real locked instruction. ARM, PowerPC and RISC-V are weakly ordered: all of them emit real instructions (dsb/dmb on ARM).
Most drivers never write barriers explicitly: locks, atomics and writel() contain them. They appear in lockless rings shared with hardware.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: atomic_t vs refcount_t vs plain int: when is each appropriate?
notes.back:
• Plain int with ++: load, add, store. Updates are lost under concurrency, volatile or not.
  • atomic_t / atomic64_t: atomic_inc(), atomic_dec_and_test(), atomic_cmpxchg(). Use for counters, flags and state machines.
  • refcount_t: for object lifetimes. It saturates instead of wrapping and warns on increment-from-zero and on underflow, turning refcount bugs from exploitable use-after-free into a leak plus a warning.
  • Bit flags: set_bit(), clear_bit(), test_and_set_bit() are atomic; the __set_bit() forms are not.
The kernel does not use C11 _Atomic / <stdatomic.h>; it has per-architecture implementations.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: What happens with C11 _Atomic on a Cortex-M0, and what is the usual alternative there?
notes.back:
ARMv6-M (Cortex-M0/M0+) lacks the exclusive-access instructions LDREX/STREX that ARMv7-M uses for lock-free atomics. The compiler emits calls to __atomic_* / __sync_* library routines, which on bare metal are frequently missing (link error) or implemented with a lock.
ATOMIC_INT_LOCK_FREE reports whether a type is lock-free.
Usual alternative on a single core: a short critical section.
uint32_t primask = __get_PRIMASK();
__disable_irq();
counter++;
__set_PRIMASK(primask);         /* restore, do not blindly enable */
Save and restore the previous state so the section nests correctly, the same idea as spin_lock_irqsave().

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: Spinlock vs mutex in the kernel: what are the context rules, and when is spin_lock_irqsave() required?
notes.back:
• mutex: a contended caller sleeps. Process context only. The holder may sleep.
  • spinlock_t: a contended caller busy-waits and preemption is disabled. Usable in any context. The holder must not sleep: no GFP_KERNEL allocation, no copy_from_user(), no mutex_lock(), no msleep().
If a lock is also taken in an interrupt handler, every process-context user must take it with spin_lock_irqsave(&lock, flags). Otherwise the interrupt can arrive on the same CPU while the lock is held and spin forever: a self-deadlock. spin_lock_bh() suffices when the other user is a softirq.
With PREEMPT_RT, spinlock_t becomes a sleeping lock; raw_spinlock_t remains a true spinlock.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: Which execution contexts exist in the kernel, and which of them may sleep?
notes.back:
• Process context (system calls, kernel threads, workqueues, threaded interrupt handlers): may sleep, unless a spinlock is held or preemption/interrupts are disabled.
  • Softirq / tasklet / timer callback: may not sleep.
  • Hard interrupt handler: may not sleep.
  • Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI): may not sleep and may not even take ordinary spinlocks.
"Atomic context" is everything that may not sleep. Violations show up as "BUG: scheduling while atomic" or "sleeping function called from invalid context".
Annotate functions that may sleep with might_sleep() so misuse is caught even when the sleep rarely happens.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: Describe Read-Copy-Update (RCU) at the API level. What is the C-level trick in rcu_assign_pointer() / rcu_dereference()?
notes.back:
Readers proceed without locks or atomic operations; updaters publish a new version and free the old one only after every pre-existing reader has finished (a grace period).
rcu_read_lock();
p = rcu_dereference(gp);        /* READ_ONCE + checks */
if (p) use(p->field);
rcu_read_unlock();

new = kmalloc(...); *new = *old; new->field = v;
rcu_assign_pointer(gp, new);    /* barrier, then publish */
synchronize_rcu();              /* or kfree_rcu(old, rcu) */
kfree(old);
rcu_assign_pointer() guarantees the object's initialisation reaches memory before the pointer becomes visible; rcu_dereference() fetches the pointer exactly once.
Readers may not block (classic RCU). Best for read-mostly data.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: What are per-CPU variables, and why must preemption be considered when using them?
notes.back:
DEFINE_PER_CPU(type, name) creates one instance per CPU: no locking, no cache-line bouncing. Typical for statistics and per-CPU queues.
Hazard: a task preempted and migrated between computing the per-CPU address and using it updates another CPU's copy, racing with that CPU.
  • get_cpu_var(x) / put_cpu_var(x): disable and re-enable preemption around the access
  • this_cpu_inc(x), this_cpu_add(x, n): a single preemption-safe operation (one instruction on x86)
  • if an interrupt handler touches the same variable, interrupts must also be disabled, or the this_cpu_* operations used

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: What is an ABBA deadlock, and how does the kernel find lock-ordering bugs before they hang a system?
notes.back:
Thread 1 takes A then B; thread 2 takes B then A. Each holds what the other needs.
Rule: define a global order for locks that nest, and always acquire in that order.
lockdep (CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING) records the order in which lock classes are acquired and reports a possible deadlock the first time an inverse order is observed, even if the deadlock never actually occurred. It also catches a lock used both with interrupts enabled and from an interrupt handler, and sleeping while holding a spinlock.
Develop drivers with lockdep enabled.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: How does a driver put a process to sleep until the hardware has data? Why is the condition an argument of the macro?
notes.back:
/* read() path */
ret = wait_event_interruptible(dev->wq, dev->data_ready);
if (ret)
        return ret;             /* -ERESTARTSYS: a signal arrived */

/* interrupt handler */
dev->data_ready = true;
wake_up_interruptible(&dev->wq);
The macro checks the condition, marks the task as sleeping, checks again, and only then schedules. That closes the lost-wakeup window where the interrupt fires between the check and the sleep. It also re-checks after every wake-up, because wake-ups can be spurious.
For a one-shot "operation finished" event use struct completion (wait_for_completion_timeout() / complete()).

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: Bare metal, single core: a 32-bit tick counter is incremented in a timer interrupt and read in main() on an 8-bit AVR. volatile is present. What is still wrong?
notes.back:
The read takes four byte-loads. The interrupt can fire between them: 0x0000FFFF → 0x00010000 may be read as 0x0001FFFF or 0x00000000. This is a torn read. The same occurs with a 64-bit variable on a 32-bit Cortex-M.
volatile only forces the loads to happen; it does not make them atomic.
Fixes:
  • read inside a critical section (save interrupt state, disable, copy, restore)
  • or read twice until both reads agree (the lock-free equivalent of a seqlock)
Any object wider than the native word, and any multi-member state, needs this treatment.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: How does a lock-free single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer work, and why is its size a power of two?
notes.back:
#define N 256u                          /* power of two */
static uint8_t buf[N];
static volatile uint32_t head, tail;    /* free-running */

/* producer (ISR) */
if (head - tail < N) { buf[head & (N - 1)] = c; head++; }
/* consumer (main) */
if (head != tail)    { c = buf[tail & (N - 1)]; tail++; }
  • each index is written by exactly one side, so no lock is needed; indices must be native-word sized so reads are not torn
  • power-of-two size: masking replaces modulo, and unsigned wrap-around keeps head - tail correct, so all N slots are usable
  • write the data first, then advance the index
Kernel: kfifo. On multi-core systems barriers are required; kfifo contains them.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: What is priority inversion, and how is it handled in a Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) and in Linux?
notes.back:
A low-priority task L holds a mutex needed by high-priority H. A medium-priority task M preempts L, so H effectively waits for M, without bound. The Mars Pathfinder resets are the textbook case.
Priority inheritance: while H is blocked on the mutex, L runs at H's priority.
  • FreeRTOS: mutexes implement inheritance; binary semaphores do not, so do not use them for mutual exclusion
  • Linux: rt_mutex, PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT; under PREEMPT_RT most kernel locks are rt_mutex based
Mitigations by design: short critical sections, and not sharing locks across widely separated priorities.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: Reentrant vs thread-safe: what is the difference, and why does it matter for interrupt handlers?
notes.back:
• Thread-safe: correct when called concurrently from several threads, typically thanks to a lock.
  • Reentrant: correct when interrupted mid-execution and entered again on the same thread. That requires no static state and no non-recursive locks.
A lock-based thread-safe function is not reentrant: if an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) interrupts the lock holder and calls the same function, it deadlocks. Hence malloc() and printf() are forbidden in an ISR.
Not reentrant: anything with static buffers (strtok(), asctime()) or a function-local static.
FreeRTOS provides separate non-blocking ...FromISR() variants of its API for this reason.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Concurrency, Atomics and Interrupt Context
notes.front: What is a seqlock, and when is it a better fit than a spinlock?
notes.back:
The writer increments a sequence counter before and after updating (the counter is odd while an update is in progress). Readers take no lock: they read the counter, read the data, and retry if the counter was odd or has changed.
do {
        seq = read_seqbegin(&sl);
        t = shared_time;
} while (read_seqretry(&sl, seq));
Good for small data that is read very often and written rarely; writers are never delayed by readers. The kernel's timekeeping uses it.
Limitation: readers must not follow pointers inside the protected data, since they may be looking at a half-updated state.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Write container_of() and explain why the kernel is built around it.
notes.back:
#define container_of(ptr, type, member) ({                      \
        void *__mptr = (void *)(ptr);                           \
        ((type *)(__mptr - offsetof(type, member))); })
Given a pointer to a member, it returns a pointer to the enclosing struct. (The real macro also statically asserts that the types match.)
It enables intrusive data structures and C-style inheritance: generic code deals only with the embedded struct list_head, struct kref, struct work_struct, struct device or struct cdev; the driver recovers its private struct in the callback.
static void foo_work(struct work_struct *w)
{
        struct foo *foo = container_of(w, struct foo, work);
}
No separate allocation per node, no void * context pointer, and the data stays cache-local.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How does the kernel's struct list_head differ from a textbook linked list? Which iterator is required when deleting during iteration?
notes.back:
It is an intrusive, circular, doubly linked list. The node (next, prev) is embedded in your struct; the list head is a node of the same type, so an empty list points to itself and there are no NULL checks.
struct foo { int v; struct list_head node; };
LIST_HEAD(foos);

list_add_tail(&f->node, &foos);
list_for_each_entry(f, &foos, node)
        pr_info("%d\n", f->v);
Deleting while iterating: list_for_each_entry_safe(f, tmp, &foos, node), which caches the next element first.
list_del() poisons the pointers (LIST_POISON1/2) so a stale use faults at a recognisable address. One object can sit on several lists by embedding several nodes. Locking is the caller's job.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How do ERR_PTR(), PTR_ERR() and IS_ERR() work? What is the classic mistake?
notes.back:
The top 4095 values of the address space (-MAX_ERRNO to -1 as unsigned long) are never valid kernel pointers, so a negative errno can be encoded in a pointer return value.
clk = devm_clk_get(dev, NULL);
if (IS_ERR(clk))
        return PTR_ERR(clk);
IS_ERR(p) is (unsigned long)p >= (unsigned long)-MAX_ERRNO.
Classic mistake: testing with if (!p). A function returns either NULL or ERR_PTR on failure; check its documentation. IS_ERR(NULL) is false. IS_ERR_OR_NULL() exists, but needing it usually indicates an unclear API.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Show the kernel's goto-based error unwinding pattern and its rules.
notes.back:
static int foo_probe(struct platform_device *pdev)
{
        int ret;

        ret = a_init();
        if (ret)
                return ret;
        ret = b_init();
        if (ret)
                goto err_a;
        ret = c_init();
        if (ret)
                goto err_b;
        return 0;

err_b:
        b_exit();
err_a:
        a_exit();
        return ret;
}
  • release in exact reverse order of acquisition
  • name labels after what they undo
  • one exit path per resource level; never jump backwards
  • remove() performs the same sequence in full
devm_* and __free()/guard() reduce the need for it, but the pattern is everywhere.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What are the kernel's return-value conventions?
notes.back:
• Actions/commands: 0 on success, negative errno on failure (-ENOMEM, -EINVAL, -EIO, -ENODEV, -EBUSY, -EFAULT, -ETIMEDOUT).
  • Predicates (pci_dev_present(), list_empty()): non-zero / true means yes.
  • Pointer-returning functions: NULL or ERR_PTR(-errno), depending on the function.
  • read()/write() handlers: byte count ≥ 0, or negative errno.
  • Interrupt handlers: IRQ_HANDLED, IRQ_NONE, IRQ_WAKE_THREAD.
Propagate the error code you received rather than inventing a new one. The negative errno travels unchanged up to the system-call boundary, where libc turns it into -1 plus errno.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What are BIT(), GENMASK(), FIELD_PREP() and FIELD_GET()? Rewrite val = (reg >> 4) & 0x7; with them.
notes.back:
#define CTRL_EN         BIT(0)
#define CTRL_MODE       GENMASK(6, 4)   /* bits 6..4 inclusive */

mode = FIELD_GET(CTRL_MODE, reg);
reg &= ~CTRL_MODE;
reg |= FIELD_PREP(CTRL_MODE, 5);
GENMASK(h, l) builds a contiguous mask and fails to compile if h < l. FIELD_PREP/FIELD_GET derive the shift from the mask at compile time, and FIELD_PREP rejects constant values that do not fit.
One definition per field, matching the datasheet, with no separate _SHIFT macro to drift out of sync.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How does kernel code guard against integer overflow in size calculations?
notes.back:
if (check_mul_overflow(n, size, &bytes))        /* also _add, _sub */
        return -EOVERFLOW;

p = kmalloc_array(n, sizeof(*p), GFP_KERNEL);   /* NULL on overflow */
p = kcalloc(n, sizeof(*p), GFP_KERNEL);
p = kmalloc(struct_size(p, items, n), GFP_KERNEL);
p = kmalloc(array_size(a, b), GFP_KERNEL);
check_*_overflow() wrap __builtin_*_overflow(): correct for any mix of integer types, no Undefined Behaviour, and compiled to a flag check.
array_size(), array3_size() and struct_size() saturate to SIZE_MAX, which no allocator can satisfy.
Pattern to eliminate: kmalloc(n * sizeof(*p), ...) with n from user space or a device. A wrapped product gives an undersized buffer and a heap overflow.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How should a driver log? Cover printk levels, pr_*, dev_*, dynamic debug, and pointer printing.
notes.back:
• printk(KERN_ERR "..."): levels 0 to 7 (EMERG, ALERT, CRIT, ERR, WARNING, NOTICE, INFO, DEBUG).
  • pr_err(), pr_info()...: shorthands. Define pr_fmt(fmt) as KBUILD_MODNAME ": " fmt before the includes to prefix every message.
  • With a struct device, use dev_err(dev, ...), dev_warn(), dev_dbg(): they prefix the driver and device name.
  • dev_dbg()/pr_debug() compile to nothing unless DEBUG is defined, or can be toggled at run time with CONFIG_DYNAMIC_DEBUG.
  • dev_err_probe(dev, ret, ...) in probe(): stays quiet for -EPROBE_DEFER and returns ret.
  • %p prints a hashed value to avoid leaking addresses; %px prints the real value (debugging only).
  • In hot or interrupt paths use *_ratelimited() or *_once().

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Show the kref reference-counting pattern. Why is the release function a callback?
notes.back:
struct foo { struct kref ref; ... };

static void foo_release(struct kref *k)
{
        struct foo *f = container_of(k, struct foo, ref);
        kfree(f);
}

kref_init(&f->ref);                     /* count = 1 */
kref_get(&f->ref);
kref_put(&f->ref, foo_release);         /* frees at 0 */
The object frees itself when the last holder drops it, whoever that is: remove(), the final close(), or a work item.
Rules: take a reference before handing the pointer to another context; never kref_get() on an object whose count may already be zero (use kref_get_unless_zero() under the lookup lock).
This is how an object outlives the hot-unplugged device while a file descriptor is still open.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: BUG_ON() vs WARN_ON(): which should a driver use?
notes.back:
BUG_ON(cond) kills the current context with an oops. Locks that were held stay held and the machine usually dies. It is essentially banned in new code.
WARN_ON(cond) prints a backtrace, taints the kernel and continues; it returns the condition, so:
if (WARN_ON_ONCE(!dev->regs))
        return -EINVAL;
Use it for "cannot happen" driver bugs and recover gracefully. Prefer the _ONCE variant to avoid flooding the log. Never make it triggerable from user space: systems running with panic_on_warn would reboot.
Expected run-time failures (bad input, hardware timeout) are not warnings: return an errno and, if useful, dev_err().

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: The kernel has no libc. Which string and parsing functions should be used, and which are deprecated?
notes.back:
Available from lib/: memcpy, memset, strlen, strcmp, snprintf, kasprintf, kstrdup, sort, bsearch.
  • copying strings: strscpy(dst, src, size): always NUL-terminates and returns the length or -E2BIG. strcpy, strncpy on NUL-terminated strings, and strlcpy are deprecated or removed.
  • parsing numbers: kstrtoint(), kstrtou32(), kstrtoul(): strict, overflow-checked, return errno. simple_strtoul() and sscanf("%d") are discouraged.
  • formatting into a buffer: scnprintf() returns the number of characters actually written (snprintf() returns what it would have written). For sysfs show() use sysfs_emit().

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How do you compare wrapping tick counters such as jiffies correctly? Give the portable embedded form as well.
notes.back:
if (jiffies > timeout) breaks when the counter wraps.
Kernel:
unsigned long timeout = jiffies + msecs_to_jiffies(100);
while (!done) {
        if (time_after(jiffies, timeout))
                return -ETIMEDOUT;
        ...
}
time_after(a, b) is ((long)((b) - (a)) < 0): unsigned subtraction wraps correctly, and the signed cast interprets the difference. Valid for intervals below half the counter range.
Bare-metal equivalent, relying only on unsigned wrap-around:
uint32_t start = millis();
if ((uint32_t)(millis() - start) >= timeout_ms) { ... }
Compare elapsed time, never absolute time stamps.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: An oops reads: "unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at 0000000000000018". What does the 0x18 tell you, and how do you locate the line?
notes.back:
The faulting address is NULL + 0x18: code accessed a member at offset 0x18 through a NULL struct pointer. Find which struct in that function has a member at offset 24 (pahole -C struct_name).
Locating it:
  • RIP: foo_read+0x3c/0x120 [foo] gives function, offset and module
  • scripts/faddr2line foo.ko foo_read+0x3c gives file:line (needs debug info)
  • or objdump -dS foo.ko, or gdb foo.ko with list *(foo_read+0x3c)
  • scripts/decode_stacktrace.sh decodes a whole log
Also read the taint flags and the call trace; entries marked ? are unreliable.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Which run-time checkers does the kernel offer for C memory and Undefined Behaviour bugs?
notes.back:
• Kernel Address Sanitizer (KASAN): out-of-bounds and use-after-free on heap, stack and globals, via shadow memory
  • Undefined Behaviour Sanitizer (UBSAN): bad shifts, out-of-bounds array indexing, misaligned access, overflow
  • Kernel Memory Sanitizer (KMSAN): use of uninitialised memory
  • Kernel Concurrency Sanitizer (KCSAN): data races
  • kmemleak: unreferenced allocations
  • lockdep: lock ordering and context misuse
  • CONFIG_DEBUG_ATOMIC_SLEEP, CONFIG_DEBUG_LIST, CONFIG_FORTIFY_SOURCE, CONFIG_DMA_API_DEBUG
  • kfence: low-overhead sampling heap checker suitable for production
Test a driver on a debug kernel with these enabled (QEMU is fine). They find what review misses.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What are the main points of the kernel coding style, and which tool checks it?
notes.back:
• tabs, 8 columns wide; more than three indentation levels suggests the function needs splitting
  • line length about 80, hard limit 100
  • opening brace on the same line, except for function definitions
  • no typedef for structs; write struct foo. Exceptions: opaque or arch-varying types (pte_t), and u8/u16/u32/u64
  • snake_case, short local names, descriptive global names
  • sizeof(*p) rather than sizeof(struct foo)
  • no casting of void *
  • functions that do one thing, with a central exit via goto
  • comments explain why; kernel-doc /** */ for exported APIs
scripts/checkpatch.pl --strict for patches; sparse and W=1 builds for semantics.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What do the attributes __must_check, noinline, __always_inline, __maybe_unused, __cold and the fallthrough; pseudo-keyword do?
notes.back:
• __must_check (warn_unused_result): warning when the caller ignores the return value; applied to many functions returning errors
  • noinline / __always_inline: override the inlining heuristics
  • __maybe_unused: suppresses unused warnings, e.g. power-management callbacks that are only referenced when CONFIG_PM is set
  • __cold: rarely executed; optimised for size and placed away from hot code
  • fallthrough;: expands to __attribute__((fallthrough)). Required for every intentional switch fall-through since the kernel builds with -Wimplicit-fallthrough
  • also: __pure, __noreturn, __aligned(n), __packed, __printf(a, b), __section(name)

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Linux Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Why does kernel style write p = kmalloc(sizeof(*p), GFP_KERNEL); without a cast and without naming the type?
notes.back:
• sizeof(*p) follows the declaration: if the type of p changes, the size remains right. sizeof(struct foo) can silently go stale and become an under-allocation.
  • sizeof does not evaluate its operand, so *p is fine even though p is uninitialised.
  • In C, void * converts implicitly to any object pointer type. A cast adds nothing and can hide a missing prototype or a wrong type.
  • Prefer kzalloc() unless every byte is about to be overwritten: it avoids uninitialised-member bugs and information leaks.
  • For arrays: kcalloc(n, sizeof(*p), GFP_KERNEL).

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Write the minimal loadable kernel module. What does each macro do?
notes.back:
#include <linux/module.h>
#include <linux/init.h>

static int __init foo_init(void)
{
        pr_info("foo: loaded\n");
        return 0;               /* non-zero: load fails */
}

static void __exit foo_exit(void)
{
        pr_info("foo: unloaded\n");
}

module_init(foo_init);
module_exit(foo_exit);
MODULE_LICENSE("GPL");
MODULE_AUTHOR("...");
MODULE_DESCRIPTION("...");
  • module_init/module_exit: entry points for insmod and rmmod
  • __init/__exit: code discarded after init / omitted when built in
  • MODULE_LICENSE: determines access to EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL symbols and kernel tainting
