Makefile: obj-m += foo.o, built with make -C /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/build M=$PWD modules. Real drivers use module_platform_driver() and friends instead of hand-written init/exit.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What are the steps to expose a character device at /dev/foo? What is the shortcut?
notes.back:
• alloc_chrdev_region(&devt, 0, 1, "foo"): reserve a major/minor number
  • cdev_init(&foo->cdev, &foo_fops); cdev_add(&foo->cdev, devt, 1): bind the numbers to the file_operations
  • class_create() + device_create(): creates the sysfs entries; udev/devtmpfs then creates the /dev/foo node
  • teardown in reverse order
Shortcut for a single node: struct miscdevice with misc_register(): major 10, dynamic minor, node created automatically.
In open(), recover the driver state with container_of(inode->i_cdev, struct foo, cdev) and store it in file->private_data.
First check whether an existing subsystem fits (IIO, input, hwmon, GPIO, tty, V4L2): a framework is preferred over a custom character device.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Give the prototype and return semantics of the read file operation. What must it do with *ppos?
notes.back:
ssize_t foo_read(struct file *file, char __user *buf,
                 size_t count, loff_t *ppos);
  • return the number of bytes transferred (may be less than count), 0 for end of file, or a negative errno
  • buf is a user pointer: copy_to_user(), and -EFAULT if it fails
  • advance *ppos when the device has a notion of position. simple_read_from_buffer() handles this for a memory buffer
  • no data available: block (wait_event_interruptible()), or return -EAGAIN if file->f_flags & O_NONBLOCK
A read() that always returns count without ever returning 0 makes cat loop forever.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: How are ioctl command numbers built, and how do you design an ioctl argument struct that works for 32-bit user space on a 64-bit kernel?
notes.back:
#define FOO_IOC_MAGIC   'f'
#define FOO_GET_STATUS  _IOR(FOO_IOC_MAGIC, 1, struct foo_status)
#define FOO_SET_CFG     _IOW(FOO_IOC_MAGIC, 2, struct foo_cfg)
The 32-bit number encodes direction (2 bits), argument size (14), magic/type (8) and sequence number (8). The direction is from user space's point of view.
Struct design for the user-space Application Binary Interface (ABI):
  • only fixed-width __u8..__u64 / __s32; no long, no pointers (carry them as __u64), no enum, no bitfields
  • explicit padding so there are no holes; align 64-bit members to 8 bytes (i386 aligns u64 to 4, x86-64 to 8)
  • reserved fields that must be zero, plus a flags word for later extension
Then .compat_ioctl = compat_ptr_ioctl suffices. Handler: unknown commands return -ENOTTY; copy the argument in once, validate it, act.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Explain the Linux device model triad of bus, device and driver. When is probe() called?
notes.back:
• A bus (platform, PCI, USB, I2C, SPI...) knows how to enumerate or describe devices and how to match them to drivers.
  • A device (struct device embedded in struct pci_dev, struct platform_device, struct i2c_client...) represents one hardware instance.
  • A driver registers a match table and callbacks.
When a device and a driver on the same bus match (PCI IDs, USB IDs, the Device Tree compatible string, ACPI ID, or name), the core calls the driver's probe(dev). remove() runs on unbind, module unload or hot-unplug.
MODULE_DEVICE_TABLE(of, foo_of_match) exports the table so udev can autoload the module. All per-device state lives in a struct allocated in probe(), never in globals: there may be several instances.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Show the skeleton of a platform driver bound through the Device Tree (DT).
notes.back:
static int foo_probe(struct platform_device *pdev)
{
        struct device *dev = &pdev->dev;
        struct foo *foo;
        int irq;

        foo = devm_kzalloc(dev, sizeof(*foo), GFP_KERNEL);
        if (!foo)
                return -ENOMEM;

        foo->regs = devm_platform_ioremap_resource(pdev, 0);
        if (IS_ERR(foo->regs))
                return PTR_ERR(foo->regs);

        irq = platform_get_irq(pdev, 0);
        if (irq < 0)
                return irq;

        platform_set_drvdata(pdev, foo);
        return devm_request_irq(dev, irq, foo_isr, 0,
                                dev_name(dev), foo);
}

static const struct of_device_id foo_of_match[] = {
        { .compatible = "acme,foo-1.0" },
        { }
};
MODULE_DEVICE_TABLE(of, foo_of_match);

static struct platform_driver foo_driver = {
        .probe  = foo_probe,
        .driver = { .name = "foo", .of_match_table = foo_of_match },
};
module_platform_driver(foo_driver);
The DT node supplies compatible, reg (register base and size), interrupts, clocks and so on. The hardware description lives outside the C code.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is the Device Tree, and how does a driver read custom properties from it?
notes.back:
A data structure describing non-discoverable hardware (System-on-Chip peripherals, devices on I2C/SPI buses). Source .dts files are compiled by dtc into a Device Tree Blob (.dtb) that the bootloader passes to the kernel. One kernel binary can thus serve many boards.
foo@40010000 {
        compatible = "acme,foo-1.0";
        reg = <0x40010000 0x1000>;
        interrupts = <GIC_SPI 42 IRQ_TYPE_LEVEL_HIGH>;
        clocks = <&clk 7>;
        acme,fifo-depth = <64>;
};
Reading a property, firmware-agnostic (works for ACPI as well):
device_property_read_u32(dev, "acme,fifo-depth", &depth);
The DT describes hardware, not policy or Linux configuration. Custom properties carry a vendor prefix and are documented in a YAML binding schema.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What are devm_* managed resources? What is the classic lifetime bug with them?
notes.back:
Resources obtained with devm_kzalloc(), devm_ioremap_resource(), devm_request_irq(), devm_clk_get()... are tied to the device binding and released automatically, in reverse order, when probe() fails or after remove() returns. Most goto unwinding disappears.
Pitfalls:
  • lifetime: devm memory is freed at unbind, but user space may still hold an open file descriptor whose file operations dereference it → use-after-free. State reachable from open files needs its own reference count.
  • ordering: a devm interrupt is released after remove() returns, so the handler can still run during remove(). Quiesce the hardware first, or free the interrupt explicitly.
  • devm is for probe()-time resources only, not for allocations made per open() or per request.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why must Memory-Mapped Input/Output (MMIO) go through readl()/writel() on an __iomem pointer rather than a plain dereference?
notes.back:
• Correct access: the accessors guarantee a single access of exactly the stated width, with the barriers the architecture requires. A plain dereference may be merged, reordered, split or widened.
  • Endianness: readl()/writel() are defined as little-endian and swap on big-endian CPUs. ioread32be() exists for big-endian devices.
  • Portability: on some architectures MMIO is not an ordinary load/store at all.
  • Checking: __iomem places the pointer in a separate sparse address space, so accidental dereferences and memcpy() are flagged. Use memcpy_toio() / memcpy_fromio().
  • Instrumentation: accessors can be traced.
Typical driver wrapper: static inline u32 foo_rd(struct foo *f, u32 off) { return readl(f->regs + off); }

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: A status register has write-1-to-clear (W1C) bits. What is wrong with writel(readl(STATUS) | IRQ_RX, STATUS);?
notes.back:
The read returns all currently pending bits. OR-ing and writing back writes a 1 to each of them, which acknowledges every pending interrupt, including ones that have not been handled. Events are lost, and only intermittently.
Correct: write only the bit(s) to be cleared.
writel(IRQ_RX, regs + STATUS);
Typical handler: stat = readl(STATUS); writel(stat, STATUS); then process exactly the bits in stat.
General rule: read-modify-write is only valid for plain read/write registers. Check the datasheet's access type for every field: W1C, read-to-clear, write-only, self-clearing. The same trap exists in microcontroller firmware: TIMx->SR |= flag; is wrong.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Write a correct interrupt handler for a possibly shared interrupt line. What must it return, and why?
notes.back:
static irqreturn_t foo_isr(int irq, void *dev_id)
{
        struct foo *foo = dev_id;
        u32 stat = readl(foo->regs + FOO_IRQ_STAT);

        if (!(stat & FOO_IRQ_MASK))
                return IRQ_NONE;        /* not ours */

        writel(stat, foo->regs + FOO_IRQ_STAT); /* ack (W1C) */
        /* minimal work: read the FIFO, complete(), wake_up() */
        return IRQ_HANDLED;
}
  • With IRQF_SHARED every handler on the line is called; each must check its own device and return IRQ_NONE if idle. The core uses this to detect and disable stuck "nobody cared" interrupts.
  • dev_id must be unique per device; it is also the key for free_irq().
  • Level-triggered: the device-side source must be cleared before returning, or the interrupt re-fires at once.
  • The handler runs in hard interrupt context: no sleeping, GFP_ATOMIC only, only spinlocks.
  • Register the handler only once everything it uses has been initialised.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Top half vs bottom half: what deferral mechanisms exist, and which would you choose for a new driver?
notes.back:
The hard interrupt handler (top half) should acknowledge the hardware, capture volatile state, and defer the rest.
  • Threaded interrupt: request_threaded_irq(irq, hard_fn, thread_fn, IRQF_ONESHOT, ...). thread_fn runs in a kernel thread and may sleep (mutexes, I2C/SPI transfers). The default choice. With hard_fn == NULL the line stays masked until the thread finishes. Mandatory for devices behind slow buses.
  • Workqueue: schedule_work() / queue_work(); process context, may sleep. Good for work not tied to one interrupt; delayed_work for timeouts.
  • Softirq: fixed set, reserved for core subsystems (networking, block, timers); network drivers use it through NAPI.
  • Tasklet: atomic context; deprecated and being removed.
  • Timers / hrtimers: atomic context callbacks.
cancel_work_sync(), del_timer_sync() and free_irq() in remove(): nothing may fire after teardown.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Direct Memory Access (DMA) API: what is the difference between coherent and streaming mappings, and what is the ownership rule?
notes.back:
Coherent (dma_alloc_coherent()): long-lived memory that the CPU and the device may access at any time without explicit synchronisation. Used for descriptor rings and mailboxes. Possibly uncached, so slower for the CPU.
Streaming (dma_map_single(), dma_map_sg(), dma_map_page()): maps an existing buffer for one transfer, with a direction: DMA_TO_DEVICE, DMA_FROM_DEVICE, DMA_BIDIRECTIONAL.
addr = dma_map_single(dev, buf, len, DMA_FROM_DEVICE);
if (dma_mapping_error(dev, addr))
        return -ENOMEM;
/* device owns buf: the CPU must not touch it */
dma_unmap_single(dev, addr, len, DMA_FROM_DEVICE);
/* CPU owns buf again */
Ownership: between map and unmap the buffer belongs to the device. The map/unmap calls perform cache flush/invalidate and bounce-buffer copies. To look at the data without unmapping: dma_sync_single_for_cpu() / _for_device().

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Which memory may be used for streaming Direct Memory Access (DMA), and what does the DMA mask do?
notes.back:
Allowed: memory from kmalloc() or the page allocator.
Not allowed:
  • stack memory (with CONFIG_VMAP_STACK it is not in the linear map, and it shares cache lines with unrelated data)
  • vmalloc() memory via dma_map_single() (not physically contiguous)
  • static/global objects in modules; .rodata
  • a small buffer embedded in a struct next to fields the CPU keeps using: cache invalidation works on whole cache lines
kmalloc() guarantees ARCH_DMA_MINALIGN alignment for this reason.
DMA mask: dma_set_mask_and_coherent(dev, DMA_BIT_MASK(32)) declares how many address bits the device can drive. If a buffer lies outside that range the core uses an Input-Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) mapping or a bounce buffer (swiotlb). Set it in probe() and check the return value.
CONFIG_DMA_API_DEBUG catches most misuse.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Your driver writes a reset bit and then calls udelay(10). On PCI Express the device is sometimes not reset in time. Why?
notes.back:
PCI Express memory writes are posted: the CPU continues as soon as the write is queued, and it may reach the device later. The delay started before the device saw the write.
Fix: read any harmless register of the same device after the write. A read is non-posted and cannot complete until the preceding writes have been delivered.
writel(CTRL_RESET, regs + CTRL);
readl(regs + CTRL);             /* flush posted write */
udelay(10);
The same flush is needed after masking interrupts, before relying on "no more interrupts will arrive".
Better than fixed delays: poll a status bit with readl_poll_timeout(addr, val, cond, sleep_us, timeout_us) from <linux/iopoll.h>.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: udelay(), usleep_range(), msleep(), fsleep(): which one when?
notes.back:
• udelay(us) / ndelay(): busy-wait. The only option in atomic context. Keep it to a few microseconds; mdelay() is almost always a design smell.
  • usleep_range(min, max): sleeps using a high-resolution timer. For roughly 10 us to 20 ms in process context. The range allows wake-ups to be coalesced.
  • msleep(ms): jiffies-based, for 20 ms and more. msleep(1) may take 10 to 20 ms depending on HZ.
  • fsleep(us): picks the right one automatically.
For "wait until the hardware signals X": not a delay at all, but an interrupt plus a completion, or readl_poll_timeout(). Every wait on hardware needs a timeout and an error path; hardware does hang.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is regmap, and why use it in an I2C or SPI device driver?
notes.back:
An abstraction for register access over any bus: regmap_read(), regmap_write(), regmap_update_bits(), regmap_bulk_read(). Created with devm_regmap_init_i2c(), devm_regmap_init_spi() or devm_regmap_init_mmio().
Benefits:
  • a single driver core supports a chip that comes in I2C and SPI variants
  • built-in locking around read-modify-write
  • register cache (fewer slow bus transfers; restore state after suspend)
  • tables for readable/writable/volatile registers
  • debugfs register dump; regmap_irq for chips with interrupt controllers
Bus transfers sleep, so such drivers need threaded interrupts and mutexes rather than hard handlers and spinlocks.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: How does a driver implement mmap() to expose device memory or a buffer to user space?
notes.back:
static int foo_mmap(struct file *file, struct vm_area_struct *vma)
{
        struct foo *foo = file->private_data;
        size_t size = vma->vm_end - vma->vm_start;

        if (vma->vm_pgoff || size > foo->mem_size)
                return -EINVAL;

        vma->vm_page_prot = pgprot_noncached(vma->vm_page_prot);
        return io_remap_pfn_range(vma, vma->vm_start,
                                  foo->mem_phys >> PAGE_SHIFT,
                                  size, vma->vm_page_prot);
}
  • device registers: io_remap_pfn_range() with non-cached protection
  • a coherent DMA buffer: dma_mmap_coherent()
  • vmalloc memory: remap_vmalloc_range(); individual pages: vm_insert_page()
Validate offset and size against the region: otherwise user space can map arbitrary physical memory. Mappings are page-granular, so everything else in the same page is exposed too. The mapping can outlive close(), so the backing memory needs proper lifetime handling.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What does returning -EPROBE_DEFER from probe() mean?
notes.back:
A resource this device depends on (clock, regulator, GPIO, reset controller, PHY, another driver's device) is not available yet because its provider has not been probed. The core puts the device on a deferred list and retries after other drivers have bound.
foo->clk = devm_clk_get(dev, NULL);
if (IS_ERR(foo->clk))
        return dev_err_probe(dev, PTR_ERR(foo->clk),
                             "failed to get clock\n");
dev_err_probe() does not log for -EPROBE_DEFER, records the reason in /sys/kernel/debug/devices_deferred, and returns the error.
Consequences: acquire all resources before touching hardware or registering interfaces, and make probe() safe to run repeatedly.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Which kernel-to-user-space interfaces exist for a driver, and when is each appropriate?
notes.back:
• Existing subsystem interface (IIO, hwmon, input, V4L2, netdev, tty, GPIO): first choice; user space already has tools.
  • sysfs attributes: simple configuration and state; one value per file, text; sysfs_emit(). It is a stable interface.
  • ioctl on a character device: structured commands and binary data.
  • read/write/poll/mmap: data streams and zero-copy buffers.
  • netlink: asynchronous events and complex configuration, mainly networking.
  • configfs: user space creates kernel objects.
  • debugfs: debugging only, no stability promise, may be absent in production.
  • procfs: legacy; not for new driver interfaces.
Anything exposed to user space becomes an interface that must not break. Design it for extension: flags and reserved fields.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What stability guarantees does Linux give for the in-kernel driver API, and for the user-space interface?
notes.back:
In-kernel API and Application Binary Interface (ABI): none. Function signatures, struct layouts and whole subsystems change between releases (see Documentation/process/stable-api-nonsense.rst). Whoever changes an API fixes all in-tree users. Out-of-tree drivers break regularly and must be rebuilt for every kernel; binary modules are tied to one exact build.
User-space ABI: stable indefinitely. System calls, ioctls, sysfs and procfs formats. "We do not break user space."
Practical consequence for embedded products: upstream the driver, or budget for forward-porting it at every kernel upgrade. Vendor Board Support Package (BSP) kernels full of out-of-tree drivers are the main reason devices remain on old, unpatched kernels.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: When is a user-space driver (UIO, spidev, i2c-dev, libgpiod, VFIO) appropriate instead of a kernel driver?
notes.back:
Suitable when: the device is simple or a one-off, latency requirements are modest, no other kernel subsystem needs it, or the logic is proprietary or needs floating point and libraries.
  • Userspace I/O (UIO): mmap() the registers, block in read() for interrupts; a tiny kernel stub only acknowledges the interrupt
  • spidev / i2c-dev: raw bus transfers from user space
  • libgpiod (GPIO character device); the sysfs GPIO interface is deprecated
  • VFIO: safe Direct Memory Access (DMA) from user space through the Input-Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU); used by DPDK/SPDK
Not suitable when: the device must work during boot, other drivers depend on it (clocks, regulators), a standard interface is expected, interrupt latency is critical, or DMA is needed without an IOMMU.
Advantages: a crash does not take the kernel down, normal debuggers work, and there is no dependence on the unstable in-kernel API.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What does runtime power management require from a driver at the C level?
notes.back:
ret = pm_runtime_resume_and_get(dev);   /* power up + usage count */
if (ret < 0)
        return ret;
/* ... access hardware ... */
pm_runtime_mark_last_busy(dev);
pm_runtime_put_autosuspend(dev);
  • runtime_suspend() / runtime_resume() callbacks in struct dev_pm_ops: gate clocks, save and restore register context
  • pm_runtime_enable() in probe(), pm_runtime_disable() in remove()
  • every hardware access must happen between a get and a put: touching a block whose clock or power domain is off causes a bus error or a hang
  • gets and puts must balance on all error paths (pm_runtime_resume_and_get() drops its reference on failure; the older pm_runtime_get_sync() does not)
  • system sleep: DEFINE_SIMPLE_DEV_PM_OPS(); quiesce interrupts and DMA in suspend()

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: Show the two standard ways of accessing a memory-mapped peripheral register in bare-metal C, and explain each keyword.
notes.back:
Single register:
#define RCC_AHB1ENR (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40023830u)
RCC_AHB1ENR |= 1u << 0;
Struct overlay, in the style of the Common Microcontroller Software Interface Standard (CMSIS):
typedef struct {
        volatile uint32_t CR1;  /* 0x00 */
        volatile uint32_t CR2;  /* 0x04 */
        volatile uint32_t SR;   /* 0x08 */
        volatile uint32_t DR;   /* 0x0C */
} USART_TypeDef;
#define USART1 ((USART_TypeDef *)0x40011000u)

while (!(USART1->SR & USART_SR_TXE)) ;
USART1->DR = c;
  • volatile: every access is a bus access with side effects; without it the polling loop becomes an infinite loop on a cached value
  • uint32_t: fixes the access width
  • integer-to-pointer cast: implementation-defined, valid on every such target
  • u suffix: keeps the constants unsigned
  • the struct must contain explicit reserved members for gaps; verify with static_assert(offsetof(...))

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: GPIOA->ODR |= (1u << 5); in the main loop, and an interrupt handler also changes pins on GPIOA. What is the bug, and what hardware features avoid it?
notes.back:
|= is load, OR, store. If the interrupt fires between the load and the store, the main loop writes back a stale value and undoes the handler's change. It happens rarely and is very hard to reproduce.
Solutions:
  • dedicated set/clear registers: a write of 1 affects only that bit, with no read involved. STM32: GPIOA->BSRR = 1u << 5; (set), GPIOA->BSRR = 1u << (5 + 16); (clear). Other vendors: OUTSET/OUTCLR/OUTTGL.
  • bit-banding (optional on Cortex-M3/M4): each bit has an alias word address, and the hardware performs the read-modify-write atomically
  • otherwise a critical section around the read-modify-write
The same analysis applies to any register or variable shared between contexts.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: What does Cortex-M hardware do on exception entry and return? What follows for writing handlers in C?
notes.back:
Entry: the hardware pushes r0-r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR (8 words, plus floating-point registers if that context is active) onto the current stack, loads the handler address from the vector table, and puts a special EXC_RETURN value (0xFFFFFFF1/F9/FD...) in lr.
Return: branching to EXC_RETURN (an ordinary bx lr) makes the hardware pop the frame and resume.
Consequences:
  • the pushed set equals the caller-saved registers of the ARM procedure call standard, so a handler is a plain void f(void) C function
  • tail-chaining: back-to-back interrupts skip the pop/push pair
  • late arrival: a higher-priority interrupt arriving during stacking is serviced first
  • the stacked pc is the key to fault debugging
Classic ARM, RISC-V, AVR and others do need __attribute__((interrupt)) or an assembly wrapper.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: How do Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC) priorities work on Cortex-M? What is the difference between PRIMASK and BASEPRI?
notes.back:
• A lower number means a higher priority. Reset, Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) and HardFault have fixed negative priorities.
  • Only the top N bits of the 8-bit priority field are implemented (often 3 or 4). NVIC_SetPriority() shifts for you; writing the raw register with an unshifted value is a classic bug.
  • A strictly higher preemption priority interrupts a running handler (nesting). The priority grouping splits the field into preemption and sub-priority.
  • PRIMASK (__disable_irq()): masks everything except NMI and HardFault.
  • BASEPRI (ARMv7-M and later, not on Cortex-M0): masks only priorities at or below a threshold, so critical high-priority interrupts keep running.
FreeRTOS uses BASEPRI: interrupts with a priority above configMAX_SYSCALL_INTERRUPT_PRIORITY (numerically lower) are never masked by the kernel, and in exchange must not call any FreeRTOS API.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: What are the design rules for an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) in firmware?
notes.back:
• Keep it short and bounded: acknowledge, move data, set a flag or notify a task, return.
  • No blocking, no busy-wait delays, no printf(), no malloc(), no non-reentrant library calls.
  • Clear the interrupt source, or the handler re-enters immediately and main() never runs.
  • Clear it early in the handler. If the clearing write is the last instruction, it may not have propagated through the bus before exception return, causing a spurious second entry. Read the register back or add __DSB().
  • Shared variables: volatile, plus a critical section on the reader side for anything wider than one native word.
  • Defer work: a flag for the super-loop, or a queue / semaphore / task notification in a Real-Time Operating System (RTOS), using the FromISR API.
  • Know the worst-case execution time; it adds directly to the latency of every lower-priority interrupt.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: A Cortex-M target ends up in HardFault_Handler. How do you find the cause?
notes.back:
• Determine which stack was active (bit 2 of EXC_RETURN in lr: MSP or PSP) and read the stacked frame: r0-r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR. The stacked pc is the faulting instruction (or the one after it); the stacked lr identifies the caller.
  • Read the fault status registers: Configurable Fault Status Register CFSR (0xE000ED28), HardFault Status Register HFSR (0xE000ED2C), and the fault addresses MMFAR / BFAR when their valid bits are set.
  • Look up the pc in the map file or with addr2line.
Usual causes: NULL or wild pointer (bus fault), access to a peripheral whose clock is off, stack overflow, calling a function pointer with bit 0 clear (INVSTATE: no Thumb bit), unaligned access with trapping enabled, divide by zero when DIV_0_TRP is set, returning from a Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) task function.
IMPRECISERR: the bus fault was reported late and pc is unreliable. Temporarily disable write buffering (DISDEFWBUF) to make it precise.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: How does a stack overflow show up on a microcontroller, and how can it be detected?
notes.back:
Without a Memory Management Unit (MMU) there is no guard page. The stack grows silently into .bss, the heap or another task's stack. Symptoms appear far from the cause: globals changing on their own, faults in unrelated code.
Detection and prevention:
  • static analysis: -fstack-usage (.su files) and call-graph tools; avoid recursion and large locals
  • stack painting: fill the stack with a pattern at start-up and check the high-water mark (FreeRTOS: uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark())
  • FreeRTOS configCHECK_FOR_STACK_OVERFLOW = 2: checks the pattern at each context switch (after the fact)
  • Memory Protection Unit (MPU) guard region below the stack: immediate fault
  • ARMv8-M Mainline stack limit registers MSPLIM / PSPLIM: hardware fault on overflow
  • place the stack at the bottom of RAM so an overflow runs into unmapped space and faults immediately
Budget for interrupts: on Cortex-M all handlers run on the main stack, nested, on top of whatever is already there.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: Why is dynamic memory allocation avoided in small embedded systems, and what replaces it?
notes.back:
• fragmentation: with kilobytes of RAM and months of uptime, a general-purpose heap eventually fails although enough total memory is free
  • non-deterministic timing of malloc() / free()
  • failure handling: there is no sensible response to NULL deep inside a control loop
  • not reentrant unless locked; leaks are fatal in a device that never restarts
MISRA C (Motor Industry Software Reliability Association guidelines): Rule 21.3 bans <stdlib.h> allocation; Directive 4.12 bans dynamic allocation in general.
Replacements:
  • static allocation of everything, sized for the worst case; the linker then proves it fits
  • allocation only during initialisation, never freed
  • fixed-block memory pools: O(1), no fragmentation, one pool per object size
  • FreeRTOS: configSUPPORT_STATIC_ALLOCATION, or heap_1 (never frees) / heap_4 (coalescing)

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: What is a watchdog timer for, and where should it be serviced?
notes.back:
An independent hardware counter that resets the system unless the software refreshes it in time. It is the last line of defence against hangs, deadlocks and runaway code.
  • Do not refresh it from a timer interrupt: interrupts keep running while the main loop is dead.
  • Refresh in the main loop or in a supervisor task, and only after verifying that every critical task has checked in since the last refresh.
  • A windowed watchdog also resets when refreshed too early, catching code stuck in a tight loop around the refresh.
  • Choose the timeout from the worst-case loop time; account for flash erase stalls and the bootloader.
  • Prefer a watchdog with its own clock; verify that a debugger halt freezes it.
  • After reset, read the reset-cause register and log it. An unnoticed watchdog reset hides a bug.
Linux: /dev/watchdog, serviced by systemd or a daemon on top of a hardware watchdog driver.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: A newly written peripheral driver reads zeros from every register and its writes have no effect (or the first access faults). What is the most likely cause?
notes.back:
The peripheral's clock is gated off (or the block is held in reset, or its power domain is down). After reset almost all peripherals on a modern microcontroller are unclocked to save power.
  • enable the clock first: e.g. RCC->APB2ENR |= RCC_APB2ENR_USART1EN;
  • some parts need a short delay or a dummy read-back after enabling the clock before the first register access is reliable
  • also enable the clock of the GPIO port and select the pin's alternate function
Depending on the chip, access to an unclocked block reads zero, is ignored, or raises a bus fault.
Linux equivalent: devm_clk_get_enabled(), the reset controller API and runtime power management in probe(). Forgetting them produces a synchronous external abort on the first readl().

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: No Floating-Point Unit (FPU): how does fixed-point Q-format arithmetic work in C? Show a Q15 multiply and its trap.
notes.back:
Qm.n: an integer interpreted as value / 2^n. Q15 (Q0.15 in int16_t) covers [-1, 1). Q16.16 in int32_t is a common general-purpose choice.
  • add/subtract: plain integer operations, given equal formats
  • multiply: the product carries 2n fractional bits, so widen first and shift back
static inline int16_t q15_mul(int16_t a, int16_t b)
{
        int32_t p = (int32_t)a * b;     /* Q30 */
        p += 1 << 14;                   /* rounding */
        p >>= 15;
        if (p > INT16_MAX)              /* -1 * -1 = +1: not representable */
                p = INT16_MAX;
        return (int16_t)p;
}
  • divide: ((int32_t)a << 15) / b
  • right-shifting a negative value is implementation-defined (arithmetic on all relevant compilers)
Software floating point costs hundreds of cycles per operation and kilobytes of library code. Also note that on a Cortex-M4F with a single-precision FPU, double arithmetic is still done in software: write 1.0f, not 1.0.

notes.front: A Cortex-M7 (or any core with a data cache) uses Direct Memory Access (DMA). Received data is sometimes stale and transmitted data sometimes wrong. Why, and what are the fixes?
notes.back:
The device reads and writes physical RAM while the CPU sees its data cache. They disagree unless they are synchronised.
  • transmit: data the CPU just wrote may still be only in the cache → clean (flush) the buffer to RAM before starting DMA: SCB_CleanDCache_by_Addr()
  • receive: the CPU may read an old cached copy → invalidate the range after DMA completes: SCB_InvalidateDCache_by_Addr()
  • cache maintenance acts on whole cache lines (32 bytes on Cortex-M7): DMA buffers must be aligned to, and padded to a multiple of, the cache line size, or neighbouring variables are corrupted
  • alternative: place DMA buffers in a region that the Memory Protection Unit (MPU) marks non-cacheable, or in tightly coupled memory if the DMA controller can reach it
This is precisely what dma_map_single() / dma_sync_*() do in Linux; on bare metal it is your responsibility.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: What is the difference between a microcontroller and an application processor from a software point of view? What does each typically run?
notes.back:
Microcontroller (MCU): Cortex-M, RISC-V, AVR. No Memory Management Unit (MMU), at most a Memory Protection Unit (MPU). Kilobytes to a few megabytes of on-chip RAM and flash, code executes in place from flash, deterministic interrupt latency, microamp sleep currents. Runs bare-metal firmware or a Real-Time Operating System (RTOS): FreeRTOS, Zephyr, ThreadX. One flat address space; a wild pointer can corrupt anything.
Application processor (MPU): Cortex-A, x86, RISC-V application cores. Has an MMU, external DRAM, caches, often several cores. Runs Linux: virtual memory, process isolation, drivers, file systems, networking. Boots in seconds, draws more power, and offers only soft real-time behaviour unless PREEMPT_RT or a companion real-time core is used.
Common architecture: both. Linux on the application cores for connectivity and user interface, a microcontroller core for hard real-time control, communicating over RPMsg or shared memory.
The C language is identical; the execution environment is completely different.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: Describe the boot chain of a typical embedded Linux system on an ARM System-on-Chip.
notes.back:
• Boot ROM (mask ROM in the chip): reads the boot-mode pins and loads the first stage from eMMC, SD, SPI flash or USB into on-chip SRAM. Secure boot verifies signatures here.
  • Secondary Program Loader (SPL) / first-stage bootloader: small enough for SRAM; initialises the DRAM controller and clocks; loads the full bootloader into DRAM. On ARMv8, Trusted Firmware-A runs around this stage and provides secure-world services.
  • U-Boot (or barebox, or UEFI): storage, network and USB drivers, environment and scripts; loads the kernel image, the Device Tree Blob (DTB) and optionally an initramfs; sets bootargs; jumps to the kernel.
  • Linux kernel: decompresses, sets up the MMU, parses the DTB, runs initcalls (driver probing), mounts the root file system.
  • init (systemd, BusyBox init): user space.
Build systems: Yocto or Buildroot. Robust field updates use A/B partitions with a boot counter and rollback.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: Super-loop vs Real-Time Operating System (RTOS): what are the trade-offs, and how does an interrupt hand work to a task?
notes.back:
Super-loop (while (1) { poll_a(); poll_b(); } plus interrupts): simple, one stack, easy to reason about. The worst-case response of any function equals the sum of all the others. Scales through cooperative state machines.
RTOS (preemptive, priority-based): every activity is a task with its own stack; the highest-priority ready task always runs. Blocking calls make sequential logic easy to write. Costs: RAM per stack, plus all the concurrency hazards: races, deadlock, priority inversion, stack sizing.
Handing work from an interrupt to a task (FreeRTOS):
void USART1_IRQHandler(void)
{
        BaseType_t woken = pdFALSE;
        uint8_t c = USART1->DR;

        xQueueSendFromISR(rx_queue, &c, &woken);
        portYIELD_FROM_ISR(woken);      /* switch now if a higher-priority task woke */
}
The task blocks in xQueueReceive(). This is the same split as top half / threaded handler in Linux.

notes.front: Low-power main loop: if (!event_flag) __WFI();. What is the race, and what is the correct Cortex-M idiom?
notes.back:
If the interrupt fires after the flag test and before Wait For Interrupt (WFI), the flag is set but the core goes to sleep anyway: a lost wake-up. The system sleeps until some unrelated interrupt arrives.
Correct idiom:
__disable_irq();
if (!event_flag)
        __WFI();        /* wakes on a pending interrupt even with PRIMASK set */
__enable_irq();         /* the pending handler runs here */
On Cortex-M, WFI wakes up when an interrupt becomes pending, even if PRIMASK prevents it from being taken. With interrupts disabled there is no window between the test and the sleep; the handler runs as soon as interrupts are re-enabled.
This is the same lost-wakeup problem that wait_event() solves in the kernel by re-checking the condition after marking the task as sleeping.

notes.deck: Deep C - Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Embedded Systems Engineering
notes.front: What must a bootloader do in C to jump to an application image on a Cortex-M?
notes.back:
#define APP_BASE 0x08008000u

void jump_to_app(void)
{
        const uint32_t *vt = (const uint32_t *)APP_BASE;

        __disable_irq();
        /* stop SysTick, disable and clear pending NVIC interrupts,
         * de-initialise peripherals and DMA the bootloader used */
        SCB->VTOR = APP_BASE;           /* relocate the vector table */
        __set_MSP(vt[0]);               /* application's initial stack pointer */
        __enable_irq();
        ((void (*)(void))vt[1])();      /* application's reset handler */
}
  • word 0 of the application's vector table is its stack pointer, word 1 its reset handler (bit 0 set: Thumb)
  • validate the image first: stack pointer within RAM, reset vector within flash, checksum or signature
  • after __set_MSP() do not touch local variables; production code does the last two steps in assembly or a naked function
  • the application must be linked for APP_BASE
  • Cortex-M0 has no Vector Table Offset Register (VTOR); Cortex-M0+ has it optionally. Without it, the vectors must be copied to RAM and remapped.
  • peripherals left running with their interrupts enabled will fire into the application's handlers before it is ready

notes.front: Where does a const object live on a microcontroller, and what is special about Harvard-architecture parts such as the 8-bit AVR?
notes.back:
On Cortex-M and other single-address-space parts: const objects with static storage and string literals go to .rodata in flash and consume no RAM. So declare lookup tables, fonts and configuration as static const. Without const they land in .data: a flash copy plus RAM.
Note that const char *names[] is a writable array of pointers and lives in RAM; const char *const names[] lives in flash.
Classic AVR has separate program and data address spaces. A normal pointer cannot address flash, so plain const data is copied to RAM at start-up. Keeping it in flash requires PROGMEM plus pgm_read_byte(), or the __flash named address space in avr-gcc.
Writing to a flash-resident object through a cast-away const is silently ignored or faults.

notes.front: What is MISRA C, and which of its rules reflect the C hazards covered in this deck?
notes.back:
Guidelines from the Motor Industry Software Reliability Association for C in safety-related systems (automotive, medical, industrial, avionics). It restricts C to a subset that avoids undefined, unspecified and implementation-defined behaviour. Rules are classed as mandatory, required or advisory; compliance is checked by static analysers, and deviations must be documented.
Examples:
  • essential type model: no implicit conversions that change signedness or narrow (Rules 10.x)
  • Rule 17.2: no recursion (bounded stack)
  • Rule 21.3 and Directive 4.12: no dynamic memory
  • Rule 11.x: restrictions on pointer casts (aliasing, alignment)
  • Rule 13.2: no dependence on evaluation order
  • Rule 12.2: shift counts within range
  • Rule 1.3: no Undefined Behaviour
  • Rule 15.5 (advisory): single point of exit
Related: CERT C (security-oriented), and functional-safety standards (IEC 61508, ISO 26262) that require such a coding standard. The Linux kernel does not follow MISRA.

notes.front: Debugging firmware without printf(): which facilities does an ARM Cortex-M target offer?
notes.back:
• Serial Wire Debug (SWD) / Joint Test Action Group (JTAG): halt, single-step, hardware breakpoints (flash-resident code needs hardware breakpoints; typically 4 to 8), data watchpoints ("who writes to this address?", the tool of choice for memory corruption)
  • GDB through OpenOCD, J-Link GDB server, or pyOCD
  • Instrumentation Trace Macrocell (ITM) over the SWO pin: printf-style output at very low cost (Cortex-M3 and above)
  • Real-Time Transfer (RTT): ring buffer in target RAM, read by the probe in the background; fast enough to use inside interrupt handlers
  • semihosting: the target's printf is executed by the debugger host; very slow, and hangs without a debugger attached
  • Embedded Trace Macrocell (ETM): full instruction trace
  • a GPIO toggle plus oscilloscope or logic analyser: the most accurate timing measurement there is
  • the Data Watchpoint and Trace (DWT) cycle counter for profiling
For field failures: store the fault registers and stacked frame in no-init RAM or flash, and report them after the reboot.
